extracted.intended_audience: general readers and prospective explorers / naturalists (Victorian-era travel audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance-informing travel or naturalist narrative that combines precise scientific and navigational observation with vivid descriptive prose, practical advice for exploration, and anecdotal or policy reflection. Applicable to field reports, travelogues, and exploratory journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise geographic and navigational detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide exact positions, bearings, longitudes/latitudes, distances, and meridian/chronometer corrections (e.g., many passages quote latitudes/longitudes to the second, meridian comparisons, and statements like 'the Glenelg will, accordingly, by my observations be in 141 degrees 02 minutes 09 seconds East').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise coordinates and navigational data to increase credibility and practical utility for other mariners/surveyors; include comparisons between observers (chronometric vs triangulation) and note chart errors for readers and navigators (e.g., 'this part of the coast is laid down ten miles too much to the eastward of Sydney'). Include tide times, set and strength (knots), and anchorage suitability where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate scientific and meteorological observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record instrument-based observations and measurements (e.g., magnetical observations, errors of chronometers, barometer readings such as 'the barometer ... stood at 29.57').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed scientific readings (magnetic observations, barometer, compass comparisons) alongside narrative to support surveying work and to inform subsequent navigational or scientific use. Note instrument comparison locations (magnetic observatories) and any calibrations or local deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actionable exploration planning and logistical advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer explicit recommendations for routes, transport, timing, and provisioning for expeditions (e.g., recommending the head of the Albert River as the best point of departure; advising use of camels and timing departures with monsoons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing routes, justify choices with distance comparisons and practical considerations (shortest approach to centre, avoid protracted expeditions). Give procurement sources and timings (where to obtain camels, seasonal monsoon advice) and list necessary arrangements for disembarkation and staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid sensory and atmospheric description
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ evocative sensory detail and dynamic weather imagery (examples: 'thick impenetrable fogs', 'a long sheet of hissing foam', 'mist-capped hills', 'dense mass of rich foliage').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, sensory language to convey atmosphere and mood; juxtapose large-scale landscape outlines (mountain ranges, horizons) with close foreground detail (trees, waterholes) to create depth and reader immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of footnotes for technical digressions and supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Place technical calculations, extended observations, policy commentary, and source clarifications in footnotes (many passages include explanatory footnotes about longitudes, local incidents, or supplementary opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep narrative flow intact while relegating dense technical data, precise measurements, and ancillary commentary to footnotes; use footnotes to document evidence, give alternative measurements, or expand on a point without interrupting the main account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend personal anecdote and reflection with empirical report
rubrics_metrics.description: Interleave personal stories, moral reflections, or eyewitness anecdotes (e.g., the squatter's hardship, the prayer during danger, turning loose rabbits) with survey and descriptive material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance objective reporting with humanizing anecdotes to provide context, illustrate consequences (social or environmental), and engage readers emotionally, while making clear what is observation versus opinion (some views are explicitly 'my own opinion').

rubrics_metrics.name: Document local ecology, fauna, and human interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Record flora and fauna (swans, a black-and-white goose, rabbits, finch species, eucalypti), indigenous and settler behavior, sealers' practices, and interactions with natives (e.g., natives seizing spears; settlers employing aborigines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specific natural-history details and social interactions to situate the place culturally and ecologically; note uses (employment of natives on whaling boats), population effects (introduced rabbits), and any measures taken by locals (scare-figures against natives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give practical maritime safety guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide warnings about reefs, sunken rocks, channels, tide streams, and anchorage limitations (e.g., 'This, Endeavour Reef, and a sunken rock ... constitute the chief dangers', 'ships should not pass' between certain extremes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List hazards, safe channels, bearings and distances from known marks, tidal set and stream rates, and best anchorages; include when certain anchorages are usable (wind-dependent) and recommended approaches until proper surveys are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use toponymy and naming as interpretive/contextual device
rubrics_metrics.description: Name features after people, friends, or events and explain naming choices (e.g., 'I named the summit ... after my friend Count Strzelecki'; 'Lighthouse Hill' suggested by conspicuous situation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the reasons behind place-names to provide historical and human context; use naming to commemorate contributors or to recommend functions (naming a hill 'Lighthouse Hill' when conspicuous and having building materials available).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include policy, economic, or improvement recommendations where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer prescriptive remarks about settlement, property rights, and infrastructure (e.g., arguments that 'the squatter ought to be allowed to purchase the land he occupies', proposals for lighthouses and convict labor to erect them, suggestions that islands be cultivated to supply prisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, accompany descriptive reporting with pragmatic recommendations for local improvement or governance, supported by observed problems and practical proposals (allotments in lieu, private contract sales, use of convict labor, lighthouse placement). Make clear when these are opinions.
